We should first ask how the Muʿtazilites defined a “generated” act, and then how they understood the responsibility that followed from it.
Different Muʿtazilite thinkers gave different definitions.
Al-Iskāfī, for example, defined it like this:

“Any act that can happen by mistake, without being deliberately intended or willed, is a generated act. Any act that can occur only through deliberate intention, and whose every part requires a renewed decision, intention, and will, falls outside the category of generated acts.”
Other Muʿtazilites defined a generated act in other ways:
“An act that happens because of something I do, but occurs in someone or something other than myself.”
“An act whose cause I brought about, after which I can no longer prevent it.”
“An act produced by an agent indirectly, as opposed to an act performed directly.”
The difference between al-Iskāfī’s definition and the others is clear.
Al-Iskāfī makes it part of the definition that the generated act happens “by mistake, without being deliberately intended or willed.”
The other definitions only require that the generated act be caused by the original or direct act, whether intentionally or accidentally.
This difference matters because it affects the question of responsibility.

If an act is defined from the start as something that happens accidentally and without intention, this tends to suggest that the person who performed the original act did not “create” the later effect.
The other definitions point in the opposite direction.
They describe the later act as something that happens “because of” the first actor, whose action “brought about its cause,” or as something that “proceeds from” that actor.
This suggests that the later act should also be attributed to the person who performed the first act.
And if so, that person is responsible for it.
The Muʿtazilites also disagreed directly over responsibility itself.
The first thinker to mention here is Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, one of the earliest thinkers to discuss generated actions.
The first kind is generated by an action whose manner the person understands.
The second also follows from the person’s action, but the person does not understand how it occurs—for example, color, taste, smell, and similar qualities.
Acts of the first kind count as human acts.
Acts of the second kind do not.
We find a clearer explanation of this distinction in al-Ashʿarī’s account of the Muʿtazilite position on human power.

According to this account, God gives human beings power over things whose manner they understand—such as movement, stillness, sounds, pain, and pleasure—because these are things human beings are capable of bringing about.
But God cannot give them power over things whose manner they do not understand—such as colors, tastes, life, death, and incapacity—because a human being cannot bring these things about.
Here the phrase “cannot bring about” appears to mean simply “is unable to bring about.”
The basic distinction seems to be between things that happen through human will and things that happen without human will playing a part in their occurrence.
From a moral or legal point of view, this distinction has a clear logic.
From a philosophical point of view, however, we will shortly see that there is more to say.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir, the leading Baghdad Muʿtazilite whom al-Shahrastānī describes as “one of the finest Muʿtazilite scholars” and as the thinker who introduced the doctrine of generated acts and “took it to an extreme,” held a different view.
“Color, taste, smell, and all forms of perception—including hearing and sight—can be generated by a human act if their causes come from that person’s action.”

If someone causes themselves or someone else to experience a sensation—such as seeing a color, tasting something, smelling something, feeling touch, or hearing a sound—then that experience can be regarded as an act produced by the person who caused it.
Everything generated by a person’s action is therefore attributed to that person because they caused it to happen.
Bishr makes no distinction here between effects in which the actor’s will directly plays a part and effects that follow without any further act of will.
So where does the difference between Abū al-Hudhayl and Bishr come from?
Al-Ashʿarī reports that Abū al-Hudhayl believed God could keep a heavy stone suspended in the air for a long time without allowing it to fall, and that the stone could remain still.
He also believed that fire and cotton could come together without the cotton burning.
Al-Ashʿarī therefore says that al-ʿAllāf “disagreed with the people of rational inquiry on this question.”

If we take this report about al-ʿAllāf at face value, the difference between his theory of generated action and Bishr’s would seem to come from Abū al-Hudhayl’s tendency to deny the principle of causality in nature and to deny the law of motion.
But denying causality would contradict one of the two principles on which the Muʿtazilite idea of generated action—and the responsibility connected with it—was built.
One of those principles was causality.
The other was human freedom of choice.
We will see, however, that there is a mistake in understanding al-ʿAllāf’s position in this way.
Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir, by contrast, clearly bases his view on the principle of causality.
In this respect, his position fits directly with the wider Muʿtazilite idea.
We find the same consistency in another leading Muʿtazilite thinker, al-Khayyāṭ.
Al-Khayyāṭ connects generated action directly to both the necessary causal order of nature and the law of motion.
He explains his position with two examples.
In the first, a person sends a stone rolling from the top of a mountain. The stone falls toward the ground. Suppose the person dies before the stone reaches the bottom.
The stone’s continued fall after the person’s death is still generated by the act of releasing it.
Its movement must therefore still be attributed to the person who set it in motion, and to no one else.
In the second example, a man shoots an arrow at a target and dies after the arrow has left the bow but before it reaches the target.
The arrow’s continued movement after the archer’s death is generated by his shot.
It therefore remains attributable to him and to no one else.
In both examples, an act begun by a person continues to produce effects after that person has died.
This gives the question two sides.
One concerns purely natural causality and, as we will see, the law of motion.
The other concerns legal and moral responsibility.
For the Muʿtazilites, however, the two cannot really be separated.

If a generated act remains attributable to the person who began the original action even after that person has died, this is because that person remains the first cause of everything that follows from the original act.
This is why Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf could say, quite literally rather than figuratively, that the dead can kill the living, healthy, and strong.
The Muʿtazilites base their judgment here on two principles.
The first is that events follow fixed laws of nature—in this case, the law of causality.
The second is that human beings are responsible for their own actions because they freely choose them.
That responsibility applies not only to acts they perform directly, but also to acts and effects generated by those direct acts.
And it is precisely the principle of causality that allows responsibility to extend from the first act to everything that follows from it.

There are also signs in some Muʿtazilite texts that they took the law of motion into account in this question. We see this especially in al-Khayyāṭ’s philosophical explanation of why the movement of an arrow should be attributed to the person who shot it.

Al-Khayyāṭ says that when someone shoots an arrow, its movement must be one of four things: an act of God, an act of the arrow itself, an act with no agent behind it, or an act of the person who shot it. He then argues against the first three possibilities and accepts only the fourth.
We can clearly see that his whole argument rests on the principle of necessary causation in nature, alongside the established Muʿtazilite principle that human beings freely choose their actions.

Al-Khayyāṭ rejects the idea that God causes the arrow to move on the following grounds. Human beings have the power to act and freely choose their actions. God does not enter into human actions or force people to perform them. If God were the one who caused the arrow to move, then a person could shoot an arrow and God could simply choose not to make it move. The arrow would then remain where it was. For al-Khayyāṭ, this is impossible.
We can see why he considers it impossible. An arrow failing to move after being shot would violate the law of motion, which necessarily requires it to move once it has been launched.

Al-Khayyāṭ says that if we accepted this impossibility, we would also have to accept many others. If God could choose not to make an arrow move after it had been shot, then we would also have to allow, for example, that an extremely strong person could press a sword against the back of someone’s neck, yet God might not cause the sword to cut it. Or fire could be brought into contact with esparto grass, yet God might not cause it to burn.

In other words, al-Khayyāṭ considers it impossible for a neck not to be cut when a sword is pressed against it with great force, or for esparto grass not to burn when it comes into contact with fire. And it is clear that these things are impossible for him because they would violate fixed laws of nature—above all the law of causation, together here with the law of motion.

Al-Khayyāṭ also rejects the second possibility: that the movement of the arrow is an act performed by the arrow itself. His reason is that an arrow is an inanimate object. It is neither alive nor capable of acting. It cannot perform an action because it has no choice, will, or knowledge.
This follows the Muʿtazilite understanding of human action, according to which an agent must possess all three: choice, will, and knowledge.

As for the third possibility—that the arrow’s movement is an act with no agent behind it—al-Khayyāṭ rejects this by saying that, if such a thing were possible, a book could exist without anyone having written it. That, he says, is impossible.
Why is it impossible? Surely the point is that a natural event cannot occur without a cause.
From everything we have seen so far, it appears that the Muʿtazilites came close to recognizing that nature has objective laws of its own and that natural events take place according to those laws.
We do not find a direct statement from them explicitly setting out this idea. But we do find statements on other subjects that come very close to expressing it.

We can return, for example, to our earlier discussion of the “indivisible part,” and to the different Muʿtazilite views on substance and accident. There we find attempts to understand the laws of nature in whatever way the knowledge available in their own time allowed.

Consider, too, a statement by al-Naẓẓām reported by al-Baghdādī. Al-Naẓẓām says that one kind of thing cannot produce two opposite kinds of action, just as fire cannot both heat and cool. In other words, each kind of body produces a particular kind of effect.

Al-Shahrastānī reports another statement by al-Naẓẓām that gives an example of how every natural body is subject to fixed laws. If a stone is pushed, it moves. Once the force of the push has run its course, the stone naturally returns to its place—that is, it does so because of its own nature.
Taken together, these two statements show al-Naẓẓām making a serious attempt to recognize that the laws of nature exist objectively.
We find similar attempts among other thinkers as well.

Muʿammar ibn ʿAbbād al-Sulamī, for example, argues that whatever occurs in bodies—motion and rest, color and taste, smell, heat and cold, moisture and dryness—is produced by the body itself according to its nature.
